# GOAL v4 — research first (adopted 2026-10-29)

Supersedes the RSI framing (archived at archive_rsi_v3/GOAL_v3_rsi.md). The policy-vs-fixed-exploration
comparison, C9 cost accounting, and gate ceremony are dropped as goals.

## Objective
Produce a result that changes how someone interprets or acts on cancer dependency
data, and get it in front of people who can use it (preprint + released code/tables).

## Lead question
**How much of the published "organoid-specific" dependency catalogue is a culture-medium
artifact rather than tumor biology, and which nominated targets are affected?**

Why this one: organoid media are lipid- and nutrient-poor compared with serum or
plasma, so dependencies that appear only in organoid screens (sterol synthesis,
possibly heme/OXPHOS/FA synthesis) may not hold in vivo, where tumors get LDL.
Two 2026 Nature papers (NextGen/Broad, Herranz-Ors/Sanger) now offer organoid
dependency catalogues, and nobody has quantified the medium-attributable share
genome-wide.

Already established (do not claim as novel): medium-not-format for SQLE/MSMO1
(Neiswender et al., Nature 2026, minipool 2x2), LDLR/SREBP sterol-starvation
physiology, Wnt-secretion dependency without exogenous Wnt.

## Deliverables
1. Per-gene medium-attribution table for every organoid-vs-2D differential dependency:
   library-matched (Humagne-CD FBS vs TSM vs organoid media), lineage-adjusted,
   and doubling/dynamic-range-aware. Flag hits as medium-attributable,
   format/biology-candidate, or unresolved.
2. Fraction of published organoid-specific hits that are medium-attributable, with
   the named targets most affected (e.g. sterol, heme, FA synthesis).
3. A doubling-corrected re-analysis of the core-essential "weakening" in dome screens
   (artifact vs biology), set against Herranz-Ors 2026.
4. Short preprint (resource/technical note scale) plus released code and tables.
5. One concrete wet-lab test proposed to a collaborator: lipid/LDL add-back or
   statin/SQLE-inhibitor potency in matched FBS vs organoid medium.

## Working rules
- Science over process: one review per finding, no cost ledgers or gate scoring.
- Novelty check (literature + your own downloaded papers) BEFORE calling anything new.
- Hold out patients for confirmation as before; report negatives plainly.
- Known confounders to always address: CRISPR library (all organoid/TSM screens are
  Humagne-CD; most FBS screens are Avana), lineage, screen dynamics/doublings, lab/batch.
     1	# Most "organoid-specific" cancer dependencies are culture-medium effects: a genome-wide attribution of the 2026 organoid dependency catalogues
     2	
     3	*Technical note / resource. Draft v2, 2026-10-29. Analysis code and tables: `src/medium_attribution_v2.py`, `generations/medium_attribution_v2_*.csv` (see release README).*
     4	
     5	## Abstract
     6	
     7	Two 2026 Nature studies (Neiswender et al., Broad/NextGen; Herranz-Ors et al., Sanger) published genome-wide CRISPR dependency catalogues for patient-derived organoids and nominated organoid-specific dependencies as candidate drug targets. Because organoid media are defined, serum-free formulations — lipid- and nutrient-poor relative to serum or plasma — some of these dependencies may reflect culture medium rather than tumor biology. Neiswender et al. showed this for sterol-synthesis genes in a 1,000-gene minipool; the genome-wide, per-gene decomposition has not been reported. Here we decompose every organoid-vs-2D differential dependency in the DepMap 26Q3 release into medium, format, and unresolved components, using organoid-medium models grown adherent (same medium, no dome), dome-vs-adherent contrasts at fixed medium, and an unrelated serum-free lineage (CNS in Tumor Stem Media), with library (Avana vs Humagne-CD), lineage, and dynamic-range adjustment, on development patients with held-out-patient confirmation. Of 449 differential dependencies, 84–85% are medium-attributable and none meet criteria for format-attributable. Among the Broad catalogue's published organoid-specific hits that replicate under lineage adjustment, 87% are medium-attributable; of Herranz-Ors et al.'s 18 headline organoid-specific core-fitness genes, the 8 that replicate are all medium-consistent (5 medium-attributable, including the SREBP/sterol axis MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2; 3 unresolved). The same attribution applies to dependency *losses*: the strongest losses are spliceosome/ribosome subunits (up to +1.2 Chronos), weaken in adherent organoid medium as much as in domes, and — for the curated ribosomal set — persist after global corrections in both assays, while Sanger organoid screens show 0.63× global depletion compression; together this implicates depletion kinetics under fewer doublings rather than complex biology. We release the per-gene attribution table so that any nominated organoid target can be checked before wet-lab investment.
     8	
     9	## Introduction
    10	
    11	Organoid dependency maps are being used to nominate targets that 2D screens miss. The interpretive risk is that "organoid-specific" conflates three differences from classical DepMap screens: 3D format (Matrigel domes), defined serum-free medium, and the Humagne-CD CRISPR library. Patients' tumors are perfused with plasma containing LDL cholesterol, fatty acids, heme/iron carriers, and Wnt ligands; organoid media supply few of these. A dependency that exists only because the medium lacks LDL will not hold in vivo.
    12	
    13	What is already established, and not claimed here: Neiswender et al. (Nature 2026) ran a paired minipool 2×2 (format × serum) and showed SQLE/MSMO1 dependency is medium-driven, concluding format does not significantly affect screen outcomes under serum-free conditions; the LDLR/SREBP sterol-starvation response is textbook physiology; Wnt-secretion dependency in Wnt-free formulations is expected. What has not been done: a genome-wide, per-gene attribution of the *published catalogues* — how many nominated hits are medium effects, which named targets are affected, whether dependency losses behave the same way, and whether the apparent weakening of core essentials in dome screens is a dynamics artifact. That is the contribution here.
    14	
    15	## Results
    16	
    17	### Design
    18	
    19	From DepMap 26Q3 CRISPR screens passing QC we formed, on development patients (a patient-level hold-out sequestered before analysis): organoid-medium dome models (n=68) and organoid-medium *adherent* models (n=9) across 9 lineages; FBS-adherent models in the same lineages (n=207); and CNS models in serum-free Tumor Stem Media vs FBS (n=29 vs 60). Per-gene library bias was removed using 27 FBS models screened with both Avana and Humagne-CD. For each gene we estimate four lineage-adjusted contrasts: D (dome organoid medium vs FBS 2D), A (adherent organoid medium vs FBS 2D — medium without dome), F (dome vs adherent within organoid medium — format at fixed medium), and S (TSM vs FBS in CNS — unrelated serum-free context). Hits (D q<0.01, |Δ|≥0.25) are flagged medium-attributable when A reproduces ≥50% of D with a 90% CI excluding 0 and F does not dominate; format-candidate when F reproduces ≥50% with q<0.05 and A/D<0.25; otherwise unresolved. All analyses on raw Chronos and on per-screen dynamic-range-normalized scores (common-essential median → −1); conclusions agree.
    20	
    21	### Most differential dependencies are medium effects, in both directions
    22	
    23	We find 240 dependency gains and 209 losses (normalized scale). 85% of gains and 84% of losses are medium-attributable; **zero genes are format-candidates** on either scale. Regression slopes of A on D are 0.88 (gains) and 0.90 (losses), versus 0.14/0.14 for F. Gains are partly generic serum-free effects (S slope 0.54: sterol, heme, fatty-acid synthesis), but losses are specific to the organoid formulation family (S slope −0.04). Held-out patients confirm the table: dev→held-out slope 0.97 (r=0.98), 100% sign concordance among medium-attributable hits, held-out adherent reproduction slope 0.88. Leave-one-out over the 9 adherent models: A-on-D slope 0.87–0.92, ≥94% of medium flags retained under any single drop (Fig. 1).
    24	
    25	Named medium-attributable gains include the sterol pathway (SQLE Δ=−0.84, adherent ratio 1.07; MSMO1 −0.81, 0.67), fatty-acid synthesis (FASN −0.42, 0.99; ACLY −0.41, 0.91), heme synthesis (ALAS1 −0.39; FECH −0.37), and Wnt secretion/reception (FZD5, LGR4, WLS; ratios 0.9–1.07, absent in TSM — consistent with Wnt-free formulations, though this conflicts with the NextGen minipool at these genes and should be treated as formulation-family-level evidence from 9 adherent models).
    26	
    27	Expression data (condition-mapped Omics TPM, same contrasts) corroborate the sterol axis on an orthogonal data type: mevalonate-pathway expression rises in organoid-medium models by median Δ +0.36 against a dependency Δ of −0.36 (SQLE expression +0.75 vs dependency −0.84; LDLR expression +0.61; pathway expression score −0.01 in FBS-adherent, +0.18 in organoid-medium adherent, +0.44 in domes) — the expected sterol-starvation signature. Heme and fatty-acid synthesis expression move oppositely (−0.47, −0.36), so expression supports the sterol mechanism specifically, not medium attribution in general (genome-wide corr(Δdependency, Δexpression) ≈ 0).
    28	
    29	An independent specificity control comes from plasma-like medium. In Rossiter et al.'s genome-wide K562 screens (RPMI vs human plasma-like medium, both with dialyzed serum), the HPLM−RPMI dependency shift is genome-wide orthogonal to our organoid contrast (r = 0.04), and SQLE moves in the *opposite* direction — less essential in plasma-like medium (Δ +0.44, differential Z +3.8) versus the strongest gain in serum-free organoid medium. Genes essential only in RPMI (relieved in HPLM) are enriched 4.6-fold for our medium-attributable set (Fisher p = 3×10⁻⁴). Medium-created dependencies are thus bidirectional and partly shared across systems, and a physiological formulation removes the sterol dependency that organoid formulation creates. (Caveats: single genome-wide line, dialyzed serum in both arms; the curated ribosomal set shows no weakening in fast-growing K562, consistent with a doublings-limited mechanism.)
    30	
    31	### Audit of the published catalogues
    32	
    33	Against the Broad study's own published organoids-vs-2D table (Mann-Whitney, unadjusted), 55% of its 285 gains (FDR<0.05, Δ<−0.25) replicate as lineage-adjusted hits on development patients; of those, 87% are medium-attributable and none format. Its 17 strictest gains (FDR<0.01, Δ<−0.5) are 16 medium-attributable, 1 unresolved. Published losses replicate at 61%, 85% medium.
    34	
    35	Against Herranz-Ors et al.'s organoid core-fitness catalogue: their calls are not threshold-fragile within their own assay (in their BAGEL binary matrix, exclusive genes are depleted in a median 80% of organoids, headline-18 in 69%, none below 25%) — the question is attribution, not call quality. Of 97 organoid-exclusive genes, 20 replicate as differential hits in Broad data — 14 gains and 6 *losses* (weakened in Broad organoids), illustrating cross-assay sensitivity of "specificity" calls. Of their headline 18 organoid-specific, non-common-essential genes (16 present in the Broad table), 8 replicate (all gains; Fig. 3): 5 medium-attributable (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP — the first four are the SREBP/sterol axis) and 3 unresolved (SCAP, adherent ratio 0.86; DDX3X and ITGB1, ratios <0.3, the only two genes in either catalogue whose point estimates lean away from medium attribution).
    36	
    37	### Core-essential weakening is a depletion-kinetics artifact class, visible differently in each assay
    38	
    39	The strongest individual losses are spliceosome and ribosome subunits (top Δ up to +1.2 raw Chronos; a small hand-picked panel median, +0.90, overstates the complex-wide effect and we do not use it). With curated BAGEL reference sets (spliceosome n=35, ribosomal n=38 in-table), Broad median Δ is +0.035 (spliceosome) and +0.146 (ribosomal) against a +0.031 essential-set baseline — i.e. weakening is concentrated in a subset of subunits (12/38 ribosomal and 7/35 spliceosome genes are medium-attributable loss hits), with ribosomal the only complex showing a clear whole-set shift. This is not whole-screen compression in Broad data: median common-essential Chronos is −1.375 in FBS vs −1.376 in domes (ratio 1.0006; Chronos rescales each screen), dome screens run *longer* (24 vs 21 days), and the ribosomal shift reproduces in adherent organoid medium (median A +0.19) with format-at-fixed-medium −0.01. In Sanger's assay (organoid LFC, supplementary table 6, 162 models, vs 930 Sanger 2D lines) organoid screens are globally depletion-compressed — reference-essential median LFC −0.96 vs −1.52 (0.63×). After scaling by essential depth, spliceosome shows no residual weakening (1.34 vs 1.11 ×depth; within-model percentile 0.018 vs 0.027, i.e. stronger in organoids), whereas ribosomal retains a residue in both metrics (1.25 vs 1.57 ×depth; percentile 0.021 vs 0.011). Proteasome, RNA-polymerase and DNA-replication sets show no residual weakening in either assay (Fig. 2). The unified reading is depletion kinetics: long-lived stable complexes need more doublings to deplete, organoid screens accumulate fewer doublings, and each assay's normalization determines how much of the effect remains visible. Recorded cumulative doublings would settle the mechanism directly, but CPD is recorded for 1 of 1,241 Broad screens in this release. Neither 2026 catalogue reports or corrects for the weakening, so absolute-threshold "organoid-specific essential" calls are confounded by it in both directions (cf. the 6 Herranz-Ors exclusives that are losses in Broad data). As a cross-system control, the mevalonate gain is visible within Sanger's assay too (within-model percentile 0.099 in organoids vs 0.394 in Sanger 2D lines), and among the headline 18, ITGB1 shows the largest Sanger organoid-vs-2D percentile shift (−0.233) of any gene our Broad analysis leaves unresolved — the strongest non-medium candidate in either catalogue.
    40	
    41	## Discussion
    42	
    43	For target nomination the practical rule is: an organoid-specific dependency in a nutrient-synthesis pathway (sterol, fatty-acid, heme) should be assumed medium-attributable until shown otherwise, because plasma supplies the end products in vivo. The sterol-axis genes on Herranz-Ors et al.'s headline list (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1/2, SCAP) are exactly this case. Conversely, DDX3X and ITGB1 survive our attribution as unresolved with point estimates away from medium, and are better follow-up candidates. Dependency losses deserve equal caution in reverse: a target that looks *less* essential in organoids (spliceosome/ribosome machinery) may simply reflect formulation-specific depletion kinetics.
    44	
    45	Limitations. The adherent organoid-medium contrast rests on 9 models across mixed formulations; per-gene ratios are correspondingly uncertain, which is why flags require CI support and why ~15% of hits remain unresolved rather than forced. Library handling rests on a 27-model Avana–Humagne-CD offset (a purely Humagne-matched sensitivity has only 5 FBS models in organoid lineages, r=0.75 with the main estimate, inconclusive alone). Formulation family and 3D-dome format cannot be separated for models that exist in only one condition; our format contrast is within-medium only. Sanger analyses use the published LFC tables (organoid table 6 and the cell-line EssMatrix, which differ in processing; we therefore lean on within-model percentiles and treat cross-matrix LFC magnitudes as secondary). CPD/doubling data are essentially absent from the release.
    46	
    47	Decisive tests. (1) LDL/cholesterol add-back in organoid-medium models should return the mevalonate dependency score from ≈−0.50 toward the FBS baseline ≈−0.10 and restore LDLR dependency. (2) Statin/SQLE-inhibitor potency should shift ≥5-fold between matched FBS and defined medium. (3) Doubling-recorded screens should test whether spliceosome/ribosome Chronos recovers per doubling. A concrete protocol for (1–2) accompanies this note.
    48	
    49	## Methods (summary)
    50	
    51	Screens: DepMap 26Q3 ScreenGeneEffect (Chronos), ScreenSequenceMap QC filters (PassesQC, not drug-treated/engineered, in combined set), ModelCondition formulation/format annotation. Formulation classes: FBS-containing; Tumor Stem Media; organoid-defined (OPAC/organoid formulations). Patient hold-out sequestered prior to analysis (`sequester_patients_v1`); all model selection and thresholds on development patients; one held-out evaluation run. Library offset: per-gene mean Humagne-CD − Avana across 27 dual-screened FBS models, applied to Avana screens. Contrasts: per-gene OLS on model-mean Chronos with lineage dummies; t-based p, Benjamini–Hochberg q per contrast. Normalization: per screen, nonessential median → 0, common-essential median → −1 (sets defined on FBS-adherent screens: 981 common essentials with >90% of screens <−0.5; 5,042 nonessentials). Ratio CIs by delta method (contrasts share the FBS baseline; independence assumption is conservative). Published tables: Broad figshare `organoids_vs_2d_gene_dependency_tests_full.csv`; Herranz-Ors supplementary table 4, sheet `organoid_core_fitness_genes`. Code: `src/medium_attribution_v2.py`, `src/medium_attribution_v2_heldout.py`, `src/sanger_direct_check3.py`; outputs `generations/medium_attribution_v2_{raw,norm,heldout_*}.csv`, `sanger_direct_check_v3.json`, `sanger_essdepth_v1.json`.
    52	
    53	## References
    54	
    55	1. Neiswender et al. A dependency map enhanced with next-generation 3D cancer models. Nature 2026. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10843-7.
    56	2. Herranz-Ors et al. A tumour-derived organoid biobank maps cancer gene dependencies. Nature 2026. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10830-y.
    57	3. DepMap 26Q3 release (Chronos gene effects, screen/model-condition metadata).
    58	4. Rossiter NJ et al. CRISPR screens in physiologic medium reveal conditionally essential genes in human cells. Cell Metab. 2021;33(6):1248-1263.e9. doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2021.02.005 (PMC8172426, Table S1).
    59	
    60	## Figures
    61	- Fig. 1 (`figures/fig1_attribution.png`): A vs D and F vs D for all hits, colored by flag.
    62	- Fig. 2 (`figures/fig2_weakening.png`): panel medians across Broad contrasts; Sanger essential depth and depth-scaled panel ratios.
    63	- Fig. 3 (`figures/fig3_catalogues.png`): flag composition of published hit lists.
    64	- Supplementary: `generations/survivor_candidates_v1.csv` (70 unresolved hits, least-medium-like first), `generations/medium_attribution_v2_loo.json`.

    61	    f = scr[scr.cls == "FBS"]
    62	    both = f.groupby("ModelID").Lib.agg(set)
    63	    both = both[both.map(lambda s: {"Avana", "Humagne-CD"} <= s)].index
    64	    h = ge.loc[f[(f.Lib == "Humagne-CD") & f.ModelID.isin(both)].index].groupby(scr.ModelID).mean()
    65	    a = ge.loc[f[(f.Lib == "Avana") & f.ModelID.isin(both)].index].groupby(scr.ModelID).mean()
    66	    return (h - a.loc[h.index]).mean(), len(both)

    69	def normalize(ge, ess, non):
    70	    """Per screen: common essentials median -> -1, nonessentials median -> 0."""
    71	    e = ge[ess].median(axis=1)
    72	    n = ge[non].median(axis=1)

    76	def contrast(Y, groups, lineage):
    77	    """OLS per gene: y ~ lineage dummies + group indicator. Returns beta, se, n1, n0."""
    78	    lin = pd.get_dummies(lineage, drop_first=True, dtype=float)
    79	    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Y)), groups.astype(float), lin.values])
    80	    XtX_inv = np.linalg.pinv(X.T @ X)
    81	    B = XtX_inv @ X.T @ Y.values
    82	    resid = Y.values - X @ B
    83	    dof = len(Y) - np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)
    84	    s2 = (resid ** 2).sum(axis=0) / dof
    85	    se = np.sqrt(s2 * XtX_inv[1, 1])
    86	    return pd.Series(B[1], Y.columns), pd.Series(se, Y.columns), int(groups.sum()), int((~groups).sum())

    89	def bh(p):
    90	    p = np.asarray(p)
    91	    o = np.argsort(p)
    92	    q = p[o] * len(p) / np.arange(1, len(p) + 1)
    93	    q = np.minimum.accumulate(q[::-1])[::-1]
    94	    out = np.empty_like(q)
    95	    out[o] = np.minimum(q, 1)
    96	    return out

    32	def contrast2(Y, groups, lineage, extra=None):
    33	    """OLS per gene: y ~ 1 + group + lineage dummies (+ extra covars). beta, se, p, ns."""
    34	    lin = pd.get_dummies(lineage, drop_first=True, dtype=float)
    35	    cols = [np.ones(len(Y)), groups.astype(float), lin.values]
    36	    if extra is not None:
    37	        cols.append(np.asarray(extra, dtype=float).reshape(len(Y), -1))
    38	    X = np.column_stack(cols)
    39	    XtX_inv = np.linalg.pinv(X.T @ X)
    40	    B = XtX_inv @ X.T @ Y.values
    41	    resid = Y.values - X @ B
    42	    dof = max(len(Y) - np.linalg.matrix_rank(X), 1)
    43	    s2 = (resid ** 2).sum(axis=0) / dof
    44	    se = np.sqrt(np.maximum(s2 * XtX_inv[1, 1], 0))
    45	    beta = pd.Series(B[1], Y.columns)
    46	    se = pd.Series(se, Y.columns)
    47	    p = pd.Series(2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(beta / se.replace(0, np.nan)), dof), Y.columns)
    48	    return beta, se, p, int(groups.sum()), int((~groups).sum())

    51	def flag_hits(tab):
    52	    """Classify D_org hits. Ratio CI by delta method (contrasts share the FBS
    53	    baseline, so independence overstates the ratio SE slightly: conservative)."""
    54	    t = tab.copy()
    55	    t["ratio_A"] = t.A_adh / t.D_org
    56	    var = (t.A_adh_se / t.D_org) ** 2 + (t.A_adh * t.D_org_se / t.D_org ** 2) ** 2
    57	    t["ratio_A_se"] = np.sqrt(var)
    58	    t["ratio_A_lo"] = t.ratio_A - 1.645 * t.ratio_A_se
    59	    t["ratio_A_hi"] = t.ratio_A + 1.645 * t.ratio_A_se
    60	    t["ratio_F"] = t.F_dome / t.D_org
    61	    hit = (t.D_org_q < 0.01) & (t.D_org.abs() >= 0.25)
    62	    same_A = np.sign(t.A_adh) == np.sign(t.D_org)
    63	    same_F = np.sign(t.F_dome) == np.sign(t.D_org)
    64	    medium = hit & same_A & (t.ratio_A >= 0.5) & (t.A_adh_p < 0.05) & (t.ratio_A_lo > 0) \
    65	        & ~(same_F & (t.F_dome_q < 0.05) & (t.ratio_F >= 0.5))
    66	    fmt = hit & ~medium & same_F & (t.F_dome_q < 0.05) & (t.ratio_F >= 0.5) & (t.ratio_A < 0.25)
    67	    t["flag"] = np.where(~hit, "not_a_hit", np.where(medium, "medium_attributable",
    68	                             np.where(fmt, "format_candidate", "unresolved")))
    69	    t["serumfree_support"] = np.sign(t.S_tsm) == np.sign(t.D_org)
    70	    return t

## GOAL v4 deliverables 1–3 (2026-10-29, medium_attribution_v2)

Per-gene attribution table (17,524 genes; library-offset corrected from 27
dual-library FBS models; lineage-adjusted; raw + dynamic-range-normalized
scales; dev patients: 68 dome + 9 adherent organoid-medium models vs 207
FBS-adherent models in 9 lineages):
`generations/medium_attribution_v2_{raw,norm}.csv`, code
`src/medium_attribution_v2.py`.

- Hits (norm scale, q<0.01, |Δ|≥0.25): 240 gains, 209 losses.
  **Medium-attributable: 85% of gains, 84% of losses; format-candidate: 0
  genes** (either scale). Slopes of adherent-same-medium effect on
  dome effect: 0.88 (gains), 0.90 (losses); dome-vs-adherent at fixed
  medium: 0.14/0.14; CNS serum-free (TSM): 0.54 gains, −0.04 losses —
  gains are partly generic serum-free effects, losses are
  organoid-formulation-family-specific.
- **Correction to "losses" bullet above:** the spliceosome/ribosome
  weakening is NOT dome-format-specific. It reproduces in adherent
  models in the same formulation family (splice panel raw Δ: dome
  +0.90, adherent +0.64, format-at-fixed-medium +0.13, TSM −0.03).
  Format-vs-medium is resolved in favor of medium for losses too
  (caveat: n=9 adherent models, mixed formulations).
- **Doubling/dynamic-range (deliverable 3, Broad side):** common-essential
  depth is identical across conditions (median essential Chronos: FBS
  −1.375, dome −1.376, org-adherent −1.405, TSM −1.390; compression
  ratio 1.0006) despite longer dome screens (24 vs 21 days). The
  weakening is therefore not global dynamic-range compression: median
  common-essential Δ is +0.035 while spliceosome/ribosome panels sit at
  +0.90/+0.64. CPD is recorded for 1 of 1,241 screens, so a true
  per-doubling correction is impossible in this release; complex-specific
  depletion kinetics (slow-turnover stable complexes) remain the open
  mechanism. Neither 2026 paper reports or corrects for this weakening.
- **Published catalogues (deliverable 2):** Broad figshare
  organoids-vs-2D gains (FDR<0.05, Δ<−0.25; n=285): 55% replicate under
  lineage adjustment on dev patients; of replicating hits **87% are
  medium-attributable, 0% format**. Strictest published gains (n=17):
  16 medium, 1 unresolved. Published losses (n=252): 61% replicate, 85%
  medium. Sanger/Herranz-Ors "organoid core fitness" exclusives (n=97):
  20 replicate as Broad differential hits (14 gains, 6 losses — i.e. 6
  are *weakened* in Broad organoids); 14 medium, 6 unresolved. Their
  headline 18 (exclusive, non-common-essential): 8 replicate, all gains;
  5 medium-attributable (MVD, IDI1, MBTPS1, MBTPS2, PNKP), 3 unresolved
  (SCAP ratio 0.86 but CI straddles criterion; DDX3X, ITGB1 ratio <0.3).
- Named medium-attributable targets (norm Δ, adherent ratio): SQLE
  (−0.84, 1.07), MSMO1 (−0.81, 0.67), FASN (−0.42, 0.99), ACLY (−0.41,
  0.91), ALAS1/FECH (heme; −0.39/−0.37), FZD5/LGR4/WLS (Wnt; ratios
  0.9–1.07, TSM ≈ 0 — formulation-family, conflicts with NextGen
  minipool per prior note).
- **Held-out confirmation** (25 reserved-patient domes, 5 adherent;
  `generations/medium_attribution_v2_heldout.json`): dev→held-out Δ
  slope 0.97, corr 0.98, same-sign 100% among medium-attributable hits;
  held-out adherent reproduction slope 0.88.
- Limitation: Humagne-CD-only sensitivity is underpowered (5 FBS models
  in organoid lineages); library handling rests on the 27-model offset.
- **Sanger assay direct check** (`src/sanger_direct_check3.py`,
  `generations/sanger_direct_check_v3.json`, `sanger_essdepth_v1.json`;
  v1/v2 scripts used the cell-line-only EssMatrix — superseded):
  organoid LFC (supp. table 6, 162 models) vs Sanger 2D lines (930).
  Mevalonate within-model percentile 0.099 in organoids vs 0.394 in 2D
  lines (cross-system gain confirmation, independent assay). Sanger
  organoid screens are globally depletion-compressed (reference-essential
  median LFC −0.96 vs −1.52, 0.63×). Depth-scaled, spliceosome weakening
  disappears (1.53 vs 1.45 ×essential-depth); ribosome keeps a residue
  (1.31 vs 1.63). In Broad Chronos (per-screen rescaled) only the
  complex-specific residue is visible. Unified reading: the weakening is
  a depletion-kinetics/doublings artifact class (slow-turnover complexes
  lag when doublings are fewer), associated with the slow-growth
  organoid-formulation condition; exact mechanism still needs
  CPD-recorded screens. Headline-18 within Sanger: ITGB1 (−0.233) and
  GNA13 (−0.238) show the largest organoid-vs-2D percentile shifts —
  ITGB1 remains the best non-medium candidate across both assays.

## Decisive next experiments (require new data)
1. Paired-format genome-wide screens at fixed medium in >=20 models
   (separates dome architecture from dome-medium family for the
   spliceosome loss; currently perfectly confounded).
2. Lipid add-back (LDL/cholesterol/B27 titration) in OPAC-grown models:
   predicts mevalonate dependency score returns toward FBS baseline
   (-0.50 -> -0.10) and LDLR dependency reappears.
3. Doubling-resolved screens (CPD recorded) in domes: predicts
   spliceosome/ribosome Chronos recovers when scored per doubling
   if depletion dynamics drive the loss; subcomplex heterogeneity
   (U2/U5/RBM39 vs U1/U2AF) predicts only partial recovery.
4. Statin/SQLE-inhibitor dose-response in matched FBS vs defined
   media: predicts >=5x potency shift in defined media.

Expression triangulation (`generations/expression_triangulation_v1.json`, condition-mapped Omics TPM): mevalonate expression median Δ +0.36 mirrors dependency Δ -0.36 (SQLE +0.75/-0.84; LDLR expr +0.61; mev expression score FBS -0.01, org-adherent +0.18, org-dome +0.44) — sterol-starvation signature confirmed on an orthogonal data type. Heme/FA-synthesis expression moves opposite (-0.47/-0.36), so expression corroborates the sterol axis specifically, not all medium gains. Genome-wide corr(D,E)~0.
- **HPLM reverse test (Rossiter et al. 2021, PMC8172426 Table S1; `generations/hplm_reverse_test_v1.json`):** K562 genome-wide RPMI+dS vs HPLM+dS (both dialyzed-serum). Genome-wide corr(HPLM-RPMI delta, Broad D_org) = 0.04 — orthogonal axes. SQLE is LESS essential in HPLM (delta +0.44, Zdiff +3.8) vs the top organoid-medium GAIN (-0.84): physiological formulation relieves, serum-free formulation creates, the same dependency. Genes essential only in RPMI (relieved in HPLM, Z>3, n=97) are enriched 4.6x for our medium-attributable set (Fisher p=3e-4; incl. SQLE, KDSR) — medium-created dependencies are bidirectional and partly shared. Mevalonate panel median delta is tiny (-0.08, z=-3.0) with within-pathway heterogeneity (HMGCR/LDLR more essential in HPLM). Ribosomal curated set shows no HPLM weakening (delta ~0) in fast-growing K562, consistent with depletion-kinetics rather than generic medium effects. Caveats: single GW line (K562), dialyzed serum both arms, focused panel too sparse (mev n=2).

item.text: The main v2 estimator uses t tests and rank-based residual degrees of freedom, as intended. I’m now checking the bigger inferential risks: pooling conditions within models, the library-offset correction, and what the shared FBS baseline means for “held-out confirmation.”

PAPER PMC13581617.xml A tumour-derived organoid biobank maps cancer gene dependencies
The multi-omics characterization of hundreds of 2D cancer cell lines and their perturbation in pharmacological and genetic screens 2 – 9  has been used to build reference maps of cancer dependencies to inform precision cancer medicines. However, the widely available set of around 1,000 human cancer cell lines 9  has limitations, including biased representation of certain cancer subtypes or absence of others, no patient-matched germline genetic data for accurately calling somatic variation, and a lack of linked patient characteristics or clinical data. Furthermore, most cell lines adapt to in vitro culture in ways that are not well understood, and reference patient-matched tumour samples are unavailable for comparisons, collectively hampering their use for pre-clinical research and discovery. Patient-derived xenograft models capture elements of the tumour microenvironment, but require specialized facilities and substantial resources, limiting broader use.
a , b , Number of fitness genes identified ( a ) and gene knockout scaled LFC values ( b ) for 162 organoids coloured by cancer type.  c , d , AUROC ( c ) and AUPR ( d ) obtained after classifying predefined essential and non-essential genes using CRISPRcleanR normalized and corrected LFCs.  e , Genetic constraint annotation for gene sets, including reference essential and non-essential genes, core fitness genes identified in cell lines (Core Cl), core fitness genes identified in organoids (Core Org), and genes analysed in biomarker analyses restricted to colorectal (COAD/READ,  n  = 85), oesophageal (ESCA,  n  = 59) or all gastrointestinal organoids (GI;  n  = 151).  f , Mean LFC values of differentially dependent genes for all gastrointestinal organoids, grouped by genetic constraint buckets. Dot colour indicates the significance of gene–biomarker associations (class A is more significant than class B, which is more significant than class C); ‘No’ indicates that no biomarker is associated. A two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used, with pairwise comparisons and FDR correction. Box plots display the median (centre line), first and third quartiles (box edges) and whiskers extend to 1.5× the interquartile range from the first and third quartiles. All CRISPR screens were performed with a minimum of  n  = 2 technical replicates.
We applied the Adaptive Daisy Model (ADaM) to define core fitness genes in organoids, and compared these with those in cell lines 9 . This identified 654 shared core fitness genes and 97 that were unique to organoids (Supplementary Table  4 ). Gene set enrichment analysis of organoid-specific core fitness genes highlighted strong associations with steroid biosynthesis (most significant: Biological Process—steroid biosynthetic process,  P  value = 1.38 × 10 −6 ; most enriched: Biological Process—isopentenyl diphosphate biosynthetic process, enrichment fold change = 667.5, Fisher’s exact test), potentially linked with a role for cholesterol in regulating intestinal stem cells and tumourgenesis 46  (Extended Data Fig.  9a  and Supplementary Table  4 ).
Genetic constraint, derived from population-scale human genome sequencing, reflects the degree to which a gene is intolerant to heterozygous variation and provides an orthogonal method to identify disease-linked or functionally important (essential) genes 47 , 48 . Core fitness genes experimentally derived from CRISPR–Cas9 screens in cell lines 9  and organoids (this study) were enriched for genetically constrained genes (high categories), as were reference lists of essential genes (Fig.  4e ). By additionally excluding genes commonly essential in cell lines (area under the curve (AUC) method), we refined our list to include 18 of 97 organoid-specific core fitness genes and annotated them with mouse knockout phenotypes and GTEx tissue-specific expression (Extended Data Fig.  9b ). Genes with low constraint and normal mouse knockout phenotype, such as isopentenyl diphosphate delta isomerase 1 ( IDI1 ), required for isoprenoid synthesis and involved in cholesterol production, may reflect cancer organoid selective fitness dependencies. Conversely, genes under high genetic constraint and with severe knockout phenotypes represent candidate core fitness genes identified in organoids—for example,  ITGB1  (Extended Data Fig.  9b,c ). Together, this integrative approach combining experimental data from organoids with genetic constraint from human populations identifies core fitness genes.
a , CRISPR–Cas9 gene knockout dependency values (LFCs) for  KRAS ,  EGFR  and  PTPN11  for COAD/READ ( n  = 85) organoids. WT, wild type.  b , IC 50  values for afatinib and gefitinib in COAD/READ organoids ( n  = 21). The dashed red line indicates the maximum drug concentration tested. A two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used with pairwise comparisons and FDR correction to compare  KRAS  G12 mutants, other  KRAS  mutants and  KRAS  wild-type organoids in  a , b .  c , Cell viability after removal of EGF from the culture medium. Data are mean ± s.d. of  n  = 6 technical replicates. Experiments were performed in biological duplicates.  d , Differential CRISPR–Cas9 gene knockout dependency values from two ESCA organoids derived from the same individual: one pre-chemotherapy organoid and another derived from tumour tissue after relapse (pair 1 in Extended Data Fig.  3a ). Gene effects are colour-coded based on whether a dependency was observed in the pre- (mauve) or post-treatment (green) organoid.  e , Differential sensitivity of the same two ESCA organoids as in  d  to two pan-RAS inhibitors (RMC-6236 and RMC-7977, mauve background), two DNMT1 inhibitors (5-azacytidine and decitabine, mauve background), and two PSMB5 inhibitors (bortezomib and ixazomib, green background). Data are mean ± s.d. of three technical replicates. Experiments were performed in biological duplicates. Box plots display the median (centre line), first and third quartiles (box edges) and whiskers extend to 1.5× the interquartile range from the first and third quartiles.
Organoids with high CRISPR-derived EGFR dependency were amongst the most sensitive to the EGFR inhibitors afatinib and gefitinib. Notably,  KRAS  wild-type and  KRAS G12X  organoids had greater sensitivity compared to  KRAS  non-G12 variants (Fig.  5b ). Upon combined EGFR and KRAS inhibition, only a subset of  KRAS G12X -mutant organoids exhibited pronounced loss of viability (combined maximal effect ( E max ) > 85%) and synergy (Bliss > 0.25), including when using the pan-KRAS(OFF) inhibitor BI-2865 (Syn/Eff in Extended Data Fig.  10a,f ), in part owing to potent monotherapy activities. Finally, a  KRAS Q61H  variant organoid was unresponsive to EGFR inhibition by either CRISPR or small molecules (Fig.  5b ). We further confirmed this by showing that EGF withdrawal from the culture medium did not reduce viability in Q61H organoids, unlike in G12X or wild-type organoids (Fig.  5c ). Collectively, the biobank and dependency map yield clinically relevant functional insights into the EGFR–KRAS–MAPK pathway, revealing substantial heterogeneity in responses to RAS and EGFR inhibition and showing that EGFR dependency varies across organoids with distinct  KRAS  variant alleles 53 .
CRISPR screens performed using the Yusa v1.1 (ref.  3 ) and MinLibCas9 (ref.  41 ) libraries were harmonized by restricting analyses to shared sgRNAs, enabling integrated downstream processing. Quality control procedures, adapted from established cell line screening pipelines 3 , were applied to assess replicate concordance, sgRNA representation and classifier performance in distinguishing essential from non-essential genes. Low-quality replicates and organoids failing predefined quality control criteria were excluded prior to further analysis. Read counts were normalized and corrected for copy-number effects using CRISPRcleanR (v3.0.1) 96 , followed by batch correction across libraries 97 . Gene-level fitness effects were estimated using BAGEL (v2) 45  with curated reference gene sets, and LFC values were scaled relative to essential and non-essential controls to facilitate cross-organoid comparability. Full details of sgRNA selection, quality control thresholds, normalization, batch correction, statistical procedures and final selection of models are provided in the  Supplementary Information .
Raw viability data were analysed independently for each project. Data were normalized per plate using negative (untreated, DMSO) and positive (MG-132, staurosporine, blank) controls. Dose-response curves were fitted using a non-linear mixed-effects model to estimate IC 50  and AUC values using the gdscIC50 R package (v1.7.3) 102 . For combination treatments, the maximum combination effect (combo_MaxE) was defined as the second-highest measured inhibition. Bliss excess was calculated as the difference between observed combination inhibition and the predicted Bliss additivity of the corresponding monotherapies. The results presented are the mean values across both projects.
Organoids were dissociated into single cells, resuspended in organoid culture medium either supplemented with or deprived of EGF, and seeded into 96-well plates over a 50:50 medium-to-ECM layer. The bottom ECM-containing layer was prepared with the same EGF condition as the overlaid medium. Cell viability was quantified using CellTiter-Glo 2.0 seven days after seeding.
PAPER PMC13664187.xml Transferability of Transcriptome-Based Gene-Dependency Models from Two-Dimensional Cancer Models to Patient-Derived Organoids: Blinded External Validation
PAPER PMC13581591.xml A dependency map enhanced with next-generation 3D cancer models
Despite advances in precision oncology, effective personalized treatments are still lacking for most patients with cancer 1 . The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap) accelerates this field by systematically identifying cancer vulnerabilities in diverse preclinical models. Data from over 1,300 cell lines have led to the discovery of new therapeutic strategies across multiple tumour types 2 . However, mapping cancer vulnerabilities using traditional cell lines has limitations, including insufficient cancer subtype representation and the impact of culture conditions on perturbation responses. Here we perform 147 genome-scale CRISPR screens and multi-omic characterizations of next-generation (NextGen) cancer models (organoids and spheroids) across 10 cancer types. This strategy enables the expansion of DepMap to cover new genomic and molecular subtypes and to identify new biomarker-associated vulnerabilities. These new models also preserve transcriptional programs that are silenced in traditional cell lines and facilitate the discovery of specific gene dependencies associated with these programs. Comparisons of traditional and NextGen cancer models enable further identification of distinct effects of growth format and culture medium on gene essentiality. The integrated dataset combines data from both model types to offer a valuable, expansive resource for exploring cancer vulnerabilities and is accessible via the DepMap portal.
We performed genome-scale CRISPR screens on 147 NextGen models using the Humagne enAsCas12a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) library 21  (Extended Data Fig.  3 ). Screen quality was comparable between NextGen models and traditional cell lines screened using spCas9 ( n  = 1,351) or enAsCas12a ( n  = 36) sgRNA libraries. Moreover, both showed clear separation of non-essential and essential sgRNA score distributions and similar receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and null-normalized mean difference (NNMD) scores (Fig.  1g  and Extended Data Fig.  4a,b ).
CNS models were screened as spheroids or on matrix-coated plates (termed ‘coat’ hereafter) and organoids were screened in Matrigel domes or in coat conditions, all in serum-free media (Supplementary Table  1 ). Gene expression and essentiality profiles were nearly identical across CNS growth formats (Pearson’s  r  = 0.996 and 0.990, respectively), and organoid gene dependencies also strongly agreed between the two conditions ( r  = 0.984; Extended Data Fig.  4c–h ). These results suggest that growth format does not significantly affect CRISPR screen outcomes under serum-free conditions. This finding is in contrast to a previous study that used serum-containing media 22 —a discrepancy that may be attributable to differences in medium composition and the comparison strategy used. All models were profiled for WGS, RNA-seq and CRISPR under identical conditions.
Next, we explored vulnerabilities tied to glial gene expression. We identified an enrichment of  CDK6  dependency in glial compared with mesenchymal models (Δdependency = –0.44,  P  = 0.013) (Fig.  3d,e ). Although this dependency ranked second in effect size, it fell short of the multiple-testing significance threshold ( q  = 0.28), which may be due to the small sample size of glial GBMs ( n  = 36) analysed. Comparisons with other NextGen models confirmed that this enrichment was driven by the glial state rather than serum-free media (Fig.  3e  and Extended Data Fig.  6e ). Encouraged by the clinical impact of CDK4 and CDK6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors on treatment outcomes, we pursued  CDK6  dependency and its associated biomarker.
To identify dependencies associated with this program, we correlated PDAC-classical/MUC scores with dependency scores of strong dependency genes (3 strong dependency classes in organoids;  n  = 3,521). The top correlated dependencies were enriched for canonical WNT signalling regulators, including  MESD  (ranked first;  r  = −0.544),  WLS  (second;  r  = −0.507),  TCF7L2  (fifth;  r  = −0.454),  FZD5  (seventh;  r  = −0.435) and  LGR4  (21st;  r  = −0.354) (Fig.  4d,e ). This association held when restricting the analysis to organoids grown with R-spondin 1 and WNT3A (Extended Data Fig.  7i ), which indicated that it was not driven solely by the presence of WNT activators in culture media. Notably, other WNT regulators (for example,  CTNNB1  and  BCL9L ) did not correlate significantly (Fig.  4d  and Extended Data Fig.  7j ), which suggests that the association is limited to selective WNT signalling components.
To better understand the combined dataset of NextGen and traditional models, we studied differences in gene essentiality between NextGen 3D organoids and traditional 2D models. We compared 3D organoids grown in Matrigel domes with serum-free media (containing EGF and FGF10) to lineage-matched 2D adherent models cultured directly on plastic with serum-containing media (referred to as 3D ( n  = 94) and 2D ( n  = 433) models, respectively). We maintained consistent culture conditions in each cohort to elucidate the effects of these conditions.
To broadly compare gene essentialities, we calculated the difference in mean dependency scores between 3D and 2D models for every gene ( n  = 16,691; excluding common essential genes), and identified gene sets (Hallmark and KEGG gene sets from MSigDB;  q  < 0.05) that were significantly overrepresented at the extremes of this difference (Fig.  5a,b ). Clustering these gene sets by component overlap (>0.3; Extended Data Fig.  8h ) merged two sets (adhesion and cytoskeleton (adhesion–cytoskeleton), and cell cycle), whereas five others (lipid metabolism, mTORC1, oxidative phosphorylation, UV response and systemic lupus erythematosus) remained separate. Fig. 5 Comparing 2D and 3D dependencies to disentangle the effects of culture conditions. a , b , Gene sets enriched for differential dependencies between 3D and 2D models ( n  = 94 (3D) and 433 (2D)). Odds ratios for the 9 significant gene sets ( q  < 0.05) overrepresented in the 200 outlier genes were plotted, clustered and coloured by gene overlap (>0.3;  a ). Mean dependency differences and their significance for individual genes (two-tailed Mann–Whitney  U- test; gene  n  = 3,521), coloured by the gene set clusters from  a  were also plotted ( b ).  c – e , Minipool screens were performed to elucidate the differing effects of growth format and culture medium. A minipool screen (250 test genes) was designed ( c ) to separate the effects of growth format (plastic versus dome) and culture medium (RPMI–FBS versus OPAC) on gene essentiality. We focused on the adhesion–cytoskeleton and lipid metabolism gene sets owing to their probable connection to the physical and metabolic culture environments, respectively. The 3D versus 2D growth format difference plausibly affects cell–cell and cell–extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions and associated dependencies 54 . By contrast, differential lipid content in media—2D models use lipid-rich RPMI supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), whereas organoid media contain only linoleic and linolenic acids and lack cholesterol—probably influences lipid-metabolism dependencies.
Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig.  5c , Extended Data Fig.  9a  and Supplementary Table  3 ). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig.  9b ).
After applying Chronos to the minipool screen data (which correlated well with genome-wide data,  r  > 0.59; Extended Data Fig.  9c ), we used linear regression to distinguish growth-format and culture-medium effects. This analysis identified seven genes for which dependencies were altered by growth formats ( q  < 0.05), including three integrin subunits ( ITGB1 ,  ITGAV  and  ITGA3 ) and two actin regulators ( NCKAP1  and  PTK2 ; Fig.  5d  and Extended Data Fig.  9d ). Eight genes also exhibited dependency changes across different media, three of which regulate lipid metabolism ( SPTLC1 ,  SPTLC2  and  SQLE ; Fig.  5e  and Extended Data Fig.  9e ).
A global analysis of the minipool screen results across the nine functional gene classes did not reveal collective enhancement or impairment of dependencies between different growth formats and media, except for a minor enhancement (Δdependency = 0.09) in the actin regulation class under RPMI–FBS conditions compared with OPAC (Extended Data Fig.  9f,g ). To capture opposing effects in gene classes (for example,  ITGB1  dependency increases whereas  ITGAV  decreases in dome culture), we analysed the variance in dependency score differences between conditions (dome versus plastic and OPAC versus RPMI–FBS). Growth format had significantly larger effects on integrin ( q  = 7.3 × 10 −5 ) and actin regulation genes ( q  = 7.2 × 10 −14 ), whereas culture medium significantly affected lipid metabolism genes ( q  = 1.5 × 10 −4 ; Fig.  5f,g ). These data demonstrate functional class-specific effects of growth format and medium.
To validate these findings, we knocked out  ITB1 ,  ITGAV ,  MSMO1  or  SQLE  in KP3 and HS766T pancreas models under 2D plastic (with RPMI–FBS) and 3D dome (with RPMI–FBS or OPAC) cultures. Cholesterol biosynthesis gene dependencies ( MSMO1  and  SQLE ) varied by medium, whereas integrin subunit dependencies ( ITGAV  and  ITGB1 ) were sensitive to growth format (Fig.  5h  and Extended Data Fig.  10a ). Immunofluorescence analyses confirmed that integrin β1 (encoded by  ITGB1 ) colocalized with FAK in 3D but not 2D cultures, whereas integrin αV (encoded by  ITGAV ) showed enhanced FAK colocalization in 2D relative to 3D cultures, which was partially due to reduced cell surface expression in 3D (Fig.  5i  and Extended Data Fig.  10b–e ). These findings align with their differential roles in cell–ECM interactions across different growth formats 55 .
We further demonstrated that growth format (3D Matrigel dome versus 2D monolayer) and medium (serum-free OPAC versus serum-containing RPMI) differentially affect gene essentiality (Fig.  5 ). Dependencies on integrin and actin genes were sensitive to growth format, whereas lipid metabolism dependencies were influenced by medium, a result that revealed gene class-specific effects. This finding highlights the distinct advantages and disadvantages of NextGen and traditional models and underscore the need to understand the limitations of each model type when studying dependencies.
The mutation calls from the WGS results were generated using Mutect2 (ref.  61 ), annotated and filtered downstream. The detailed strategies are described in a publicly shared document ( https://storage.googleapis.com/shared-portal-files/Tools/25Q3_Mutation_Pipeline_Documentation.pdf ). In short, variants were aligned to the GRCh38.p14 human genome assembly ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000001405.40/ ) and mutation calling was conducted with the following parameters: default format of VCF and HG38; Gatk_docker: broadinstitute/gatk:4.2.6.1; M2_extra_args:–genotype-germline-sites true–genotype-pon-sites true for getting access to germline calls; Filter_funcotations to False PoN: gs://gatk-best-practices/somatic-hg38/1000g_pon.hg38.vcf.gz; Run_funcotator to True; Run_orientation_bias_mixture_model_filter to True. The pipeline was run such that no bait sets were needed.
Cell lines with Cas activity above 70% were selected for screening. However, some lines were screened with activity as low as 44% if they showed sufficiently rapid growth of at least one population doubling per week.
gDNA samples were prepared from the screen pellets using a KingFisher Apex System (Thermo Fisher, 5400940). After preparing gDNA samples, the DNA concentration of each sample was measured using a Qubit4 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher,  Q33238 ), and the presence of library DNA was confirmed by performing PCR with a set of library-specific primers. gDNA samples were subsequently submitted for library DNA amplification and sequencing to the GPP at the Broad Institute. PCR and sequencing were performed in accordance with the ‘sgRNA/shRNA/ORF PCR for Illumina Sequencing’ protocol available at the Broad Institute GPP web portal ( https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols ). DNA samples were sequenced at a scale matched with the size of the screen: 68 µg gDNA per replicate for screens with 500× representation and 134 µg gDNA per replicate for screens with 1,000× representation.
CNS models were tested for the growth format and seeding density that resulted in optimal growth rates and for polybrene sensitivity, which was used at a concentration that resulted in >85% survival. For growth testing, cells were plated in both Matrigel-coated and ULA 6-well tissue culture plates. Specifically, cells were seeded in duplicate at densities of 100,000, 200,000 and 300,000 cells per well for both the Matrigel-coated plates and ULA plates. Cells were allowed to grow for 7 days, with a medium change performed at day 3 or 4 as needed. After 7 days, cells from all the conditions were counted and a doubling time was calculated for each condition. The condition that gave the lowest doubling time while maintaining high cell viability was used for the screen. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standardized concentration of 50 µg ml –1  and 3 µg ml –1 , respectively. For enAsCas12a transduction, 1.5 × 10 6  cells were exposed to lentivirus expressing enAsCas12ain a 24-well ULA plate in the presence of the optimized concentration of polybrene. At 18 h after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and the cells were plated in the optimal growth format at 2× the optimal seeding density. Subsequently, cells were selected with blasticidin. A CellTiter-Glo cell viability assay (CTG; Promega, G7572) was carried out 14 days after infection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to measure the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus.
For the CRISPR screens of the traditional cancer cell lines with the enAsCas12a sgRNA library (Humagne-CD), the cell lines were first tested for doubling time and cell size. Blasticidin and puromycin were used at a standard concentration of 40 μg ml –1  and 2 μg ml –1 , respectively. To infect adherent cells with lentivirus expressing enAsCas12a (Addgene, 136476), 5 × 10 6  cells were exposed to the virus in a T175 flask (Corning, 354487) in the presence of 4 µg ml –1  polybrene. For suspension cells, 1.8 × 10 7  cells were exposed to the virus in a 12-well plate (Corning, 3513) in the presence of 4 µg ml –1  polybrene, which was followed by centrifugation at 930 g , 37 °C for 2 h. One day after infection, cells were washed with PBS to remove the virus and cells were then plated at around 50% confluence. Blasticidin was added to the medium 2–3 days after infection. A CTG assay was carried out after 3 days of blasticidin selection to ensure efficient elimination of uninfected cells with blasticidin and to estimate the infection rate from the enAsCas12a virus. Cells were maintained in blasticidin for at least 10 days after transduction and throughout the screening process. After enCas12a transduction and blasticidin selection, enCas12a activity was assessed as described in the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’.
All screens were initially evaluated for sequencing quality and selected to have a mean of at least 185 reads per gene. Naive gene effect scores were calculated by taking the log of the ratio of normalized reads for each gene in screened samples to that of normalized reads for each gene in the corresponding plasmid library. For screens using the two Humagne C and D libraries, the log fold change scores of libraries were averaged together. An ROC-AUC was calculated on the basis of per cent of true positive hits (essential genes with log fold change below –1) for every possible false discovery rate. An NNMD was calculated for each screen by taking the difference between the average log fold changes for essential and non-essential genes and dividing by the standard deviation of the non-essential genes 69 . Screens that had an NNMD greater than –1.25 or a correlation between replicates less than 0.19 were excluded from downstream analyses. Chronos scores were then calculated using the open-source code Chronos (v.2.0.8;  https://github.com/broadinstitute/chronos ) as previously described 23  for each type of guide library (Avana spCas9, KY spCas9 or Humagne CD enAsCas12a) independently. To mitigate batch effects between guide libraries, the mean Chronos score per gene in individual libraries was regularized towards the global mean across all libraries. On the DepMap portal, the file ‘ScreenGeneEffect’ contains Chronos gene effect estimates for each individual screen, with library effects corrected out whereas organoid-specific effects are preserved. Beginning with the 26Q1 release, a similar strategy will be used to preserve organoid-specific effects in ‘CRISPRGeneEffect’, which integrates all screens of the same model into a model-indexed table that can be used with portal tools.
Lentiviral production was conducted using 293FT cells (Thermo Fisher,  R70007 ) in accordance with the ‘Lentiviral Production in Flasks’ protocol available at the Broad Institute GPP web portal ( https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/protocols ). In brief, the lentiviral particles were generated by the co-transfecting the lentiviral plasmid with a packaging plasmid (psPAX2; 12260, Addgene) and VSV-G envelope (pMD2.G; Addgene, 12259) into 293FT cells using PEIpro transfection reagent (Polyplus, 101000033). The medium was replaced 12 h after transfection, and the virus-containing medium was collected after 36–48 h.
For the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig.  5a,b ). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome,  https://adhesome.org/ ); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig.  9a . We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table  3 ). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool ( https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public ), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening.
Before screening, models were tested for their growth in an alternative medium (1:1 OPAC organoid medium for 2D models and RPMI with 10% FBS for 3D organoids) and with alternative growth format (3D Matrigel dome growth for 2D models and 2D monolayer growth for 3D organoids) for at least two passages. Only the combination of medium type and growth format that enabled a comparable rate of growth with the original conditions (<2-fold difference in the doubling times) and reasonably rapid growth (doubling time <120 h), as well as the original conditions of growth format–culture medium pair, were used for the screening. Moreover, all the models selected for screening were subjected to titrations of library virus and puromycin to determine the dose of virus to achieve optimal infection rates and the concentration of puromycin to kill uninfected cells within 3 days, respectively.
For the screen, selected models were infected with the amount of library virus required for infecting 30% of the cells in accordance with the result of virus titration on day 0. The infected cells were selected with the concentration of puromycin determined in the puromycin titration between day 1 and day 4. On day 4, cells were seeded into up to 4 conditions (2D monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS (RPMI–FBS); plastic culture with 1:1 OPAC; 3D Matrigel dome culture (dome culture) with RPMI + 10% FBS; and dome culture with 1:1 OPAC), depending on how many conditions survived the above-mentioned selection criteria for the respective model. For plastic culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 10 ml of the respective medium and seeded on a Falcon 100 mm TC-treated cell culture dish (Corning, 53003). For dome culture, 2 million cells were resuspended with 0.5 m of the medium used for the condition and subsequently mixed with 1.5 ml of Matrigel. Approximately 40 domes, each with 50 µl of Matrigel–cell suspension were placed on a 100 mm TC-treated culture dish, which was followed by the incubation of the plate at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the Matrigel to solidify. Subsequently, 10 ml of the culture medium was added before further incubation. We prepared two technical replicates per each condition.
Minipool screens were evaluated for sequencing quality by having a total read count of at least 500,000 reads across replicates. Gene scores and NNMDs were computed in the same manner as the genome-wide screens. Replicate correlation was computed as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient over log fold changes in all non-control genes. Screens with NNMDs greater than –1.5 and replicate correlations less than 0.2 were excluded from downstream analyses. Screens with a single replicate were retained if their other metrics passed these quality control thresholds. Chronos scores were calculated as previously described 23 , with adjusted hyperparameters (smoothing regularization parameter = 0.3, kernel width = 5) for the smaller library size. The first term captures the baseline viability effect of knocking out gene  g . The second and third terms capture the growth format effect and medium effect, where  I d  and  I s  are indicator variables representing the types of growth format (Matrigel dome culture (dome) versus monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic)) and culture medium (serum-free OPAC medium versus serum-containing RPMI–FBS medium), respectively. To assess the effects of growth format (or culture medium) on the core functional classes of gene targets included in our minipool library, we calculated the variance in  β d  (or  β s ) across members of the same class and compared it to the variance in  β d  (or  β s ) across all non-control genes outside of class. For each gene set, we tested whether the in-class variance was significantly greater than the out-of-class variance using one-tailed  F -tests.
On day 10, the medium of the plastic-cultured cells was replaced with 100 μl per well of fresh RPMI with 10% FBS, and 40 μl per well of CTG assay reagent was subsequently added. Following incubation at RT for 30 min with constant shaking, luminescence emission was measured using a SpectraMax M5 Multi-Mode microplate reader (Molecular Devices, M5). For the dome-cultured cells, the medium was replaced with 350 μl per well of fresh RPMI with 10% FBS and 350 μl per well of 3D CTG assay reagent was subsequently added. Following incubation at RT for 30 min with constant shaking, the dissolution of Matrigel was confirmed by microscopy. Next, 150 μl of the lysate was transferred to an opaque 96-well plate to measure luminescence emission via a microplate reader. The luminescence signal from each of the experimental wells was normalized using a scale in which the average value of the cutting control wells (six wells; triplicate wells for each of sgCh2 and sgAAVS1) was scored as 0 and the average value for the common essential control wells (nine wells; triplicate wells for each of sgPOLR2D, sgSF3B1 and sgKIF11) was scored as −1. The normalized viability score for each of the experimental wells was plotted. The relative viability scores before normalization were also plotted (Extended Data Fig.  10a ). The experiments were repeated twice. Each of these experiments was conducted with technical replicates ( n  = 3).
For immunostaining of cells grown in either plastic culture or the dome culture conditions, cells were propagated on a Nunc 8-Well Lab-Tek chamber slide (Thermo Fisher, 177402). For plastic culture, the slide was first incubated with 100 μg ml –1  collagen I (Corning, 354236) and 20 μg ml −1  laminin (SouthernBiotech, 1415-01) for 60 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, 20,000 cells were seeded with 200 μl RPMI with 10% FBS per well. For dome culture, 30,000 cells were resuspended with 30 μl Matrigel and placed as a dome at the centre of a well of an 8-well chamber slide. After incubating at 37 °C for 30 min to solidify Matrigel, 200 μl RPMI with 10% FBS was added to the well before further incubation. Fixation and staining were performed essentially as previously described 57 . In brief, after 3–5 days of culture, cells were washed twice with PBS before fixation. Plastic-cultured cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT. Dome-cultured cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde and 0.2% glutaraldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT, washed twice with PBS and incubated with 0.2% sodium borohydride for 30 min at 4 °C for the quenching of glutaraldehyde. For both plastic and dome cultures, this fixation procedure was followed by two washes with PBS and two rounds of incubations with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 10 min for the quenching of paraformaldehyde. After permeabilizing the cells with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 min on ice, the slides were incubated with IF buffer (0.1% BSA, 0.2% Triton-X, 0.05% Tween-20 and 0.05% NaN 3  in PBS + 10% normal goat serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 005-000-121)) for 1 h at RT for blocking. For dome culture, slides were additionally incubated with M.O.M. blocking reagent (Vector Laboratories, MKB-2213-1) for 1 h at RT to reduce endogenous mouse IgG staining of Matrigel. Subsequently, the slides were incubated with primary antibody diluted in IF buffer overnight at RT. After washing with TBS-T (0.05% Tween-20 in TBS) 3 times for 10 min each at RT, slides were incubated with secondary antibody diluted in IF buffer for 1 h at RT. This was followed by washing with PBS-T 4 times for 10 min each at RT and then the slides were incubated with PBS containing 1 μg ml –1  4′6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI; MilliporeSigma, D9452) and Phalloidin-iFluor 647 conjugate (Cayman Chemical, 20555; 1:1,000 dilution) for 30 min at RT for nuclear counterstaining and enhancement of F-actin staining, respectively. For post-fixation, slides were incubated with 1% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 5 min at RT, washed with PBS and incubated with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 5 min. Finally, cover glasses (no. 1.5) were mounted on the slides with ProLong Gold Antifade mountant (Thermo Fisher,  P36930 ). The following primary and secondary antibodies were used for the staining: anti-FAK (MilliporeSigma, 05-537 (4.47, mouse); 1:200 dilution); anti-FAK (MilliporeSigma, 06-543 (rabbit); 1:200); anti-integrin β1 (BD Pharmingen, 556048 (HUTS-21); 1:50); anti-integrin αV (MilliporeSigma, AB1930; 1:500); goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11001; 1:500); goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11008; 1:500); goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody Alexa Fluor 568 (Thermo Fisher, A-11004; 1:500); and goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 568 (Thermo Fisher, A-11011; 1:500).
The cell surface expression levels of integrin β1 and integrin αV in cells grown in either plastic or dome conditions were analysed by flow cytometry. For this, KP3 cells were grown in either plastic or dome conditions in RPMI with 10% FBS for 5 days. For collection, cells were first washed with PBS twice. Plastic-cultured cells were subsequently detached from the plate by incubating with 5 mM EDTA–PBS for 10 min at 37 °C and collected. Dome-cultured cells were collected by scraping and centrifugation. The pellets containing cells and Matrigel were resuspended in 5 mM EDTA–PBS and incubated at RT for 30 min with continuous rotation to dissolve Matrigel. Subsequently, cells were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at RT, washed twice with PBS and incubated with 0.1 M glycine in PBS at RT for 10 min twice for the quenching of paraformaldehyde. The cells were then incubated with 10% normal goat serum–PBS for 1 h at RT for blocking. For primary antibody staining, 1 × 10 6  cells were incubated at RT for 1 h with one of the following antibodies, all diluted in 10% normal goat serum–PBS: anti-integrin β1 (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank (DSHB), AIIB2; 1:40 dilution); anti-integrin αV (DSHB, P3G8; 1:58); rat IgG1κ isotype control (Thermo Fisher, 14-4301-82; 1:1,000); or mouse IgG1κ isotype control (Thermo Fisher, 14-4714-82; 1:500). This was followed by three washes with PBS for 10 min each at RT with continuous rotation and secondary antibody staining, during which cells were incubated at RT for 1 h with one of the following antibodies, all diluted in 10% normal goat serum–PBS: goat anti-rat IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11006; 1:500); or goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher, A-11001; 1:500). The cells were then washed with PBS three times for 10 min each at RT with continuous rotation and analysed by flow cytometry, which was conducted on a CytoFLEX S flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) (Extended Data Fig.  10c,d ).

Five pairs of genome-wide and minipool screens (KP3 plastic versus RPMI–FBS; HS766T plastic versus RPMI–FBS; UWB1289 plastic versus RPMI–FBS; PANFR0185T2 dome versus OPAC; and HCMBROD115C16 dome versus OPAC), for which these two types of screens were conducted under the same culture conditions (growth format and culture medium), were evaluated.
For Extended Data Fig.  9d,e , for the seven pairs of minipool screens that were conducted with the same model, same medium but different growth format (dome versus plastic), the Chronos dependency scores of all the test genes in the minipool library ( n  = 250) were compared using two-tailed paired  t -tests (d). Similarly, for the five pairs of minipool screens that were conducted with the same model, same format but different culture medium (OPAC versus RPMI–FBS), the Chronos dependency scores of all the test genes in the minipool library were also compared using two-tailed paired  t -tests (e). All genes with significant differential dependencies in either of these comparisons as well as  CDK4  and  GPX4  are shown in the plots.
For Extended Data Fig.  9f,g , effects of growth formats (f) and culture media (g) on gene dependencies (calculated by a linear regression model (see the section ‘Minipool screen analysis’ of the  Methods )) were compared between in-class genes and out-of-class genes (that is, the rest of the 250 test genes in the minipool library) for each of the 9 core functional classes of the minipool library. Significance of the difference was assessed by two-tailed Mann–Whitney  U- test. The numbers of genes in each of the 9 core functional classes are as follows: actin regulation,  n  = 75; adherens junction,  n  = 30; cell cycle,  n  = 53; ECM adhesion,  n  = 89; integrin,  n  = 22; lipid metabolism,  n  = 20; PI3K–mTOR signalling,  n  = 20; tight junction,  n  = 34; and WNT signalling,  n  = 29.
